title: Bahasa pasar — talk like a local
goal: Peel off the textbook layer and put on the street layer — the register that never appears in the newspapers but is spoken at every mamak table. Without it you can read Malaysia but you can't hear it.
bekal: recognizing and using twenty everyday contractions
using sentence-final particles (*lah, kan, kot, je, pun, ke*) without overdoing them
knowing the limits: when not to use street Malay

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Hanging out at the mamak
dialogs.intro: Eleven at night. Haziq, Aina and Sarah are sitting at an outdoor table of a mamak stall. This dialogue is written exactly as it sounds — not as it's spelled.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Weh, korang nak order apa? Aku belanja malam ni.
lines.id: Hey, what do you guys want to order? It's on me tonight.
lines.literal: hey, you-guys want order what? I treat night this.

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.text: Eh serius? Aku nak roti telur ngan teh o ais.
lines.id: Oh, seriously? I'll have roti telur and an iced black tea.
lines.literal: eh serious? I want roti egg with tea o ice.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Aku pun sama je. Tapi kenapa tiba-tiba belanja?
lines.id: Same for me. But why are you suddenly treating us?
lines.literal: I also same just. but why suddenly treat?

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Takde apa. Baru dapat duit biasiswa. Lagipun korang selalu tolong aku.
lines.id: No reason. Just got my scholarship money. Besides, you guys always help me.
lines.literal: not-have what. just get money scholarship. besides you-guys always help me.

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.text: Alaa, sweetnya. Eh, esok ada kelas tak?
lines.id: Aww, so sweet. Hey, is there class tomorrow?
lines.literal: aww, sweet-the. eh, tomorrow have class not?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Ada kot. Aku tak check lagi jadual.
lines.id: I think so. I haven't checked the timetable yet.
lines.literal: have maybe. I not check yet timetable.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Camne boleh tak check? Esok ada quiz woi!
lines.id: How can you not have checked? There's a quiz tomorrow, man!
lines.literal: how can not check? tomorrow have quiz hey!

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.text: Relaks la. Bab satu ngan dua je. Senang.
lines.id: Relax. Just chapters one and two. Easy.
lines.literal: relax lah. chapter one with two just. easy.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Senang bagi kau la. Aku baru baca separuh.
lines.id: Easy for you. I've only read half.
lines.literal: easy for you lah. I just read half.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Jom balik awal. Aku ajar kau kejap.
lines.id: Let's head back early. I'll teach you for a bit.
lines.literal: let's return early. I teach you moment.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Serius? Kau memang terbaik. Thanks weh.
lines.id: Seriously? You're the best. Thanks, man.
lines.literal: serious? you indeed best. thanks hey.

notes: ⚠️ **This dialogue uses *aku* and *kau*** (I, you) — on purpose. The three are close friends. With people you've just met, officials or older people, these words are **rude**. The gap between *saya/awak* and *aku/kau* is sharp in Malaysia; don't cross it until the other person crosses it first.

**Korang** = you guys (from *kau orang*, "you people"). Its cousins: **diorang** = they (from *dia orang*), **kitorang** = we, excluding you (from *kita orang*). All three are purely spoken forms that never appear in formal writing, and all three are very common.
**Weh** (also written *wei*, *woi*) is a call to a friend — like "hey" or "bro". Fine between friends, rude to strangers.
**Camne** = *macam mana* = how. This contraction is so common that many young people type it that way in messages. Its cousins: **camtu** (*macam tu*, like that), **camni** (*macam ni*, like this).
**Mampus aku** is a half-joking cry of panic — "I'm dead", "I'm done for". Rude when aimed at others (*mampus kau!*), but harmless about yourself.

grammars.title: Twenty contractions you must recognize
body: This is the table you most need to memorize in the whole module, even more than the false friends. The reason is simple: without it you won't catch a single sentence of real conversation, even if you know every word in its full form.
after: The pattern isn't random: almost all of them **drop the first syllable** (*sekejap* → *kejap*, *sahaja* → *je*) or **swallow a middle sound** (*macam mana* → *camne*, *dengan* → *ngan*). Once you see the pattern, you can guess short forms you've never heard.
⚠️ Keep **tak** and **tanak** apart: *tak nak* (two words) often comes out as one sound, *tanak*. *Saya tanak pergi* = "I don't want to go".

grammars.title: Sentence-final particles: tone you can write
body: Spoken Malay puts feelings at the **end of the sentence**, not just in the tone of voice. English does something similar with tags like "right?", "though", "lol" — the idea is familiar; you just need the words.
after: ⚠️ The most common learner mistake: **using too much *-lah*.** Because *-lah* is the best-known Malay particle, newcomers stick it onto every sentence and end up sounding like they're doing an impression. Malaysians use *-lah* with care; the particles you'll actually hear most are **kan**, **je** and **tak**.
Particles can **stack**: *Sedap je kan?* ("Pretty tasty, right?"), *Takde apa je pun.* ("It's nothing, really.") There's no rigid order; follow what you hear.

sections.title: The same sentence, three levels of formality

blocks.text: The best way to feel the gap is to see the same sentence written three times:

Notice that it's not only contractions that change but **the whole choice of words**: *adakah* → *tak* at the end, *memahaminya* → *faham*, *perkara* → dropped entirely. Formal Malay uses long, affixed forms; street Malay drops almost all affixes.

blocks.title: Safe rules for newcomers
items: **Start in the middle.** The "polite" register in the middle column is safe in 95% of situations — shops, class, counters, new friends.
**Go up to formal** for: emails, forms, government officers, much older people, meetings.
**Go down to street** only after the other person goes down first. It's an unwritten rule, but people keep it.

⚠️ **Don't copy swear words** from social media or TV dramas. Malay swear words sound much harsher to Malaysian ears than their translation suggests, and as a foreigner you get no social leeway for using them.
**When in doubt, use the full form.** Sounding a little stiff costs far less than sounding rude.

blocks.text: **Syok** (also spelled *shiok*, from Malay-Hokkien) is one of the most typically Southeast Asian words — used in Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei for anything that feels great: food, weather, an afternoon nap. *Syok betul!* There's no exact English equivalent.

You don't need to use a single word from this table. But you do need to **recognize** them, because this is what you'll really hear at the next table — and recognizing them is the difference between following a conversation and just waiting for your turn to speak.
